Abstract and Keywords 1.1 Abstract The Graph Coloring Problem is a conventional optimization problem in NP-hard class with relevant applications in resource management in networks, scheduling, register allocation, and frequency assignment. This paper presents an overview of the ten major algorithmic categories of approaches to solve the GCP problem including learning-based optimization, heuristic search, and meta-heuristic search, plus exact algorithms. Classical methods are addressed such as Branch-and-Bound and Backtracking/DSATUR together with constraint-driven heuristics including Minimum Remaining Values with Forward Checking and meta-heuristics that included Genetic Algorithms, Ant Colony Optimization, and Tabu Search. There is a trade-off between optimality and scalability that is clear from the literature. Exact methods guarantee optimality but have an exponential runtime. Meta-heuristic and hybrid modeling methods are returning faster, near-optimal solutions on difficult and large graphs. Learning-based methods demonstrated rapid scalability and adaptability. This work compares knowledge-guided evolutionary computation to a deterministic search through a Backtracking Search Algorithm and a Cultural Algorithm. This group specifically shows how the more recent literature on graph coloring is beginning to shift towards adaptive, data-driven optimization. Keywords Graph Coloring Problem, Backtracking Search, DSATUR, Meta-heuristics, Cultural Algorithms 2. Introduction 2.1 Problem Statement The Graph Coloring Problem has been a challenge in graph theory for a long time. A set of to circled colors assigned to the vertices of a graph where no 2 same-colored vertices are connected to each other with a line while using the least amount of colors possible. The number of total colors used is known as (Chromatic Number). The determination of the least amount of colors possible is an NP problem "nondeterministic polynomial-time" (the proposed solution can be verified quickly but for which finding the solution may be very slow). This means that there is no particular algorithm is optimal for the coloring graph, as the size of the graph increases the number of colored vertices combinations increases exponentially. There is other alternatives as backtracking, branch-and-bound, and integer programming can be useful but all of the when it comes to efficiency they lack it (Lewis & Palmer, 2025) . Therefore the graph coloring challenge has become a benchmark for algorithms optimization recent studies continued to emphasize the relevance of this problem (Lewis & Palmer, 2025). The focus of this paper is to try to propose solutions using AI algorithms to make coloring graphs better. The research goal is to show how AI algorithms can be a great solutions for the graph coloring problem. 2.2 Motivation and Significance The Graph Coloring Problem is significant because it shows real world optimization problems that require no obstacles with allocation while having limited resources. For example, in wireless networks, frequencies assigned to transmitters must avoid clashing with one another exactly like vertex coloring, no color should interfere with itself. According to IEEE survey in 2025 over 70% of spectrum management algorithms in 5G networks use graph based networks (Dai et al., 2025). Showing that graphs have significant importance to everyday uses. Also in timetabling and scheduling have concepts that rely on the same idea of coloring graphs that no tasks interfere with each other in the same time, the time here acts as the colored vertex. Beyond its uses, graph coloring stays one of the most enduring NP problems in algorithmic studies, it has great challenges in scalability and adaptability. Traditional non AI algorithms fails to effectively solve large graphs. Recent research shows that the potential of AI and metaheuristic algorithms is better to achieve faster and optimal results (Karaboğa & Kaya, 2024). Solving graph coloring through AI not only makes the understanding of optimization better but also gives benefits for industries that rely on the same theme or idea of graph coloring 2.3 Scope of This Review The research focuses on emphasizing how AI can serve the purpose of improving the graph coloring it examines both seminal works from the 2000s and the 1900s and recent research papers from the 2020s period. Those research papers show how AI can improve the algorithm. However this research does not focus purely on graph coloring proofs but it also focuses on algorithms with AI based optimization. 3. Literature Review 3.1 Overview and Classification of Approaches The approaches our group picked can be divided or classified into four main categories: exact algorithms, constraint- based heuristics, meta-heuristic methods, and hybrid or learning-based models. Exact methods give us optimal colorings through the pruning and systematic exploration. They are only suitable for smaller graphs since they have limitations by exponential time complexity. On the bright side, they are highly accurate. Constraint-based heuristics make the classical backtracking better and more improved by picking the most constrained variables first and reducing domains early. Works well and effectively for medium-sized constraint networks, since they are lightweight. Meta-heuristic approaches are optimal and scalable. They use randomness and adaptive memory, or swarm behavior to escape local minima. They are good for larger graphs. Lastly, hybrid and learning-based models incorporate knowledge-driven behavior and learned heuristics. They are scalable and robust, and work good for large and complex graph instances. 3.2 Detailed Review of Selected Approaches 3.2.1 Approach 1(Salma): Backtracking/ Depth-First Search Reference: Brélaz, D. (1979). New methods to color the vertices of a graph. Communications of the ACM, 22(4), 251–256. https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/359094.359101 Classification: Foundational / Exact Overview and Context In 1979, Brélaz introduced the Degree of Saturation (DSATUR) algorithm, a depth-first backtracking heuristic for the Graph Colouring Problem (GCP). GCP seeks the minimum number of colours to be used by which adjacent vertices are differently coloured. Brélaz proposed a heuristic method to order the vertices with the aim of reducing the search space since the problem was NP-complete. The majority of heuristic and exact coloring algorithms were built on top of DSATUR. Algorithm Description Algorithm Description DSATUR dynamically chooses the vertex that is not colored with the highest saturation degree, which basically is the number of different colors among its colored neighbors. Ties are broken by vertex degree. The saturation degree values of its neighbors are updated, and the selected vertex is given the smallest possible color. Backtracking occurs only when there is no legal color available in order to effectively prune the search tree (Brélaz, 1979). Figure 1 [4] This is a graph example that Brelaz (1979) used to demonstrate DSATUR coloring Pseudocode (adapted from Brélaz (1979)) Input: Graph G(V,E) Output: Valid coloring 1. Order vertices by decreasing degree. 2. Color the first vertex with colour 1. 3. While uncolored vertices remain: a. Select vertex v with maximum saturation degree.  b. Assign v the smallest permissible colour.  c. Update neighbours’ saturation degrees.Return colouring Experimental Setup(from the paper) It was compared to Welsh-Powell (1967), Matula et al. (1972), Dunstan (1975), and Tehrani (1975) on 55 randomly generated graphs of densities between 0.26 and 0.82. CPU time and color count were also in the metrics. Reported Results DSATUR obtained near-optimal solutions (<2 % deviation) and was computationally more efficient than earlier heuristics. it was precise and true for bipartite graphs. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Simple, efficient, and eﬀective for dense graphs; forms a foundation of many modern exact coloring algorithms. Limitations: non-parallel structure; worse performance on sparse or large graphs; exponential worst-case complexity. 3.2.2 Approach 2 (Salma): Brand and Bound (New DSATUR-Based Exact Algorithm) Reference: San Segundo, P., Rodríguez-Losada, D., & Jiménez, A. (2016). A new DSATUR-based algorithm for exact vertex coloring. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0305054811002966?via%3Dihub Classification: Recent / Exact (Branch-and-Bound Algorithm) Overview and Context In this paper, San Segundo et al. (2016) revisit Brélaz's (1979) DSATUR framework to develop a modern B&B exact solver for GCP. Recognizing the inefficiency of DSATUR's backtracking search on large graphs, the authors introduce tighter bounding rules, faster data structures, and a design suitable for parallelization. Their objective was to preserve DSATUR's user-friendly saturation-based logic while creating an exact solver that matched or outperformed commercial tools. Algorithm Description The technique incorporates the dynamic vertex ordering of DSATUR into a B&B structure. Each node represents a partial coloring, where the branching is guided by saturation degree.While greedy colorings maintain upper bounds on the chromatic number, maximal cliques give lower bounds. Whenever partial solutions surpass the best-known bound, branches are cut off. While incremental feasibility checks and compact color encoding further reduce computational overhead, a depth-first search ensures memory efficiency (San Segundo et al., 2016). Pseudocode (adapted from San Segundo et al., 2016) procedure COLOR(G, current_coloring, UB) if all vertices colored: UB ← min(UB, colors_used) return select vertex v with highest saturation degree for each feasible color c ≤ UB: assign(v, c) if colors_used + lower_bound(G, current_coloring) < UB: COLOR(G, current_coloring, UB) unassign(v) Experimental Setup(from the paper) The Benchmarks are: DIMACS COLOR02 suite (e.g., DSJC250.5, le450_25a). The Hardware: Intel Core i7 3.4 GHz, 16 GB RAM, single thread. Baselines include the traditional DSATUR, PASS, and B&C versions. Metrics include number of instances solved to optimality, node expansion, and execution time. Reported Results The new DSATUR-B&B solver, with an average speedup of 4× over classical DSATUR, 2× over PASS, reduced memory usage by half, while optimally coloring 62 out of 67 DIMACS instances. On a single core, it scaled to graphs with about 1000 vertices. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Ensures precise chromatic numbers; highly optimized implementation; significant runtime improvement through tight bounds and incremental updates. Limitations: Memory usage rises on dense graphs; worst-case time is still exponential; currently single-threaded without parallel execution. 3.2.3 Approach 3 (Alyaa): Constraint Satisfaction Heuristic (MRV + Forward Checking) Reference: D. Frost and R. Dechter, “In search of the best constraint satisfaction search,” in Proc. AAAI, Seattle, WA, USA, 1994, pp. 301–306. [6] https://www.aaai.org/Papers/AAAI/1994/AAAI94-046.pdf Classification: Foundational | Heuristic Search Overview and context The MRV + FC technique leverages the Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic and Forward Checking (FC) pruning in order to optimize backtracking search in constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), similar to Graph Coloring. MRV + FC operates on the idea of making the "hardest" choice first (MRV) and being able to quickly prune conflicts (FC) in order to reduce the size of the search tree. Recent work [17] examines the impact of propagation (the domain reductions created by FC) in both dynamic heuristics [17] in general. Algorithm Description The MRV + FC method works as a variable-ordering and lookahead technique. • MRV (Variable Ordering): MRV selects the unassigned variable with the fewest remaining values. Taking a fail-first approach, the MRV variable is the variable that places sufficient restrictions on all values, thus increasing the likelihood of failure early on and reducing branching factor. • FC (Lookahead): After assigning a value to a variable, FC immediately propagates by removing that value from all directly adjacent neighbors (i.e. the unassigned values). This light propagation essentially guarantees at a minimum, local consistency will exist immediately and removes any breakages in consistency that would eventually lead to failure on later assignments. Pseudocode Experimental Setup (paraphrased from the papers) • Van der Marel et al. (2024) studied whether information flow (domain pruning like FC) yields dynamic heuristics in CSP search [17]. • Prestwich (2002) included FC into local search neighborhoods for graph coloring and evaluated them using geometric and equipartite graphs [18]. • Abuluaih et al. (2018) compared MRV+ as an improvement to MRV baseline on 10,000 Sudoku problems [19]. Reported Results Heuristics for the reduction of the domain drastically reduced searching effort compared to lexical ordering. Table 2 demonstrates that the median search nodes for heuristics for reduction of the domain were much less (439,935) than lexical ordering (2,775,788). This provides evidence of the principal lesson learned through MRV/FC: with domain information you can search better. • Improvement for Heuristics: Prestwich (2002) noted FC improved reduced coloring in local search neighborhoods [18]. • Reduction: MRV+ (2018) exhibited marked improvements in reducing recursive calls and backtrack during evaluation of the Sudoku benchmarks [19]. • Current Work: Our most recent work [17] substantiated propagation (FC or other) can be an effective navigational lead/guide for producing dynamic heuristics in search [17]. Critical Analysis Benefits: •Reduced Search Space: Highly powerful pruner because it facilitates fail-first approaches and discovers conflicts early on. •Light Overhead: FC is lightweight look-ahead providing quite favorable overhead versus benefit. •Composite Use: Integrates well into systematic backtracking and hybrid techniques. Weaknesses: •Weaker Pruner: FC reduces local consistency (it only uses direct neighbors) and therefore cannot discover inconsistencies further out like Arc Consistency. •Overhead Cost: Maintaining domains adds per node cost, and increased benefit is strongly based on problem structure and inconsistency level discovered. •Sensitive to Ties: Standard MRV performance is affected by ties in the MRV heuristic; therefore, developing rational tie-breaking strategies is crucial. 3.2.4 Approach 4 (Alyaa): Reference: Y. S. Kalandaragh, “Speeding up the Arc Consistency algorithm in Constraint Satisfaction Problems: A new modification of AC-3,” J. Algorithms Comput., vol. 54, no. 1, pp. 125–138, Jun. 2022. [7] Classification: Recent Paper (2020-2025) | Category: Exact Search Optimization Overview and Context Arc Consistency (AC)enforced through the AC-3 algorithms used to establish local consistency in CSPs by applying that every value in the domain of each variable is supported in the domains of its neighboring variables. This allows for strong domain pruning and for early detection of infeasibility. AC-3 is most used as a preprocessing step or to complement other methods, such as when implemented in a hybrid way in MAC. Recent work [7] is aimed at addressing the high computational burden of using AC-3. Algorithm Description AC-3 is a propagation algorithm driven by a queue: • Revision Loop: First, the algorithm builds a queue containing all of the constraint arcs in the CSP. • Pruning: The operation of REVISE(X, Y) removes any values from the domain of X that could not possibly be consistent with any value in the domain of Y. • Propagation: For each domain reduction, all incoming arcs are put back on the queue, allowing the propagation of any consistency revision until there are no more available revisions (i.e., the algorithm has reached a fixed point). Figure 3 Pseudocode Experimental Setup (for AC-3 Modification – Based on Kalandaragh 2022) In [7], the authors assess the modified AC-3 algorithm with a benchmark of traditional CSP datasets comprised of conventional graph-coloring problems and Radio Link Frequency Assignment Problems (RLFAP). The experiments look at the modified AC-3 against baseline AC-3 in terms of: • Domain reduction ratios (Tables 3 - 4) • Discriminability measurements (Table 5) • aggregates for checks for total consistency and implications for revises The evaluation included runs of AC-3 in stand-alone form and hybrids incorporating MAC (Maintaining Arc Consistency) measures to evaluate improvement in pruning depth and Reported Results AC methods create reliable pruning with improved problem structure: Pruning Validation: Tables 3 and 4 show strong correlations between problem variables and domain reductions, supporting prunability reliability. Discriminability Gain: Table 5 shows increasing consistency significantly increases mean discriminability (i.e., 1.757 to 4.014^{+} with RLFAP100). This supports stronger propagation creates a more informative search space. Efficiency & Hybrid Gains: Hybrid algorithms with an integrated MAC performed significantly better than previous research implementations for robust graph coloring. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Advantages: · Superior Pruning: Results in stronger inference than FC: greater domain reduction along with a deeper look at inconsistency. · Enhanced Search Quality: Effort-saving through high discriminability (Table 5) and resultant problem simplification produced efficiencies for later search. Disadvantages: · High Computational Cost: The revision process becomes time-consuming on a per-propagation-step basis compared to FC. · Cost-Benefit: There should be some payoff if the pruning returns cost to overhead; the tradeoff may be different for the structure of the problem. · Incomplete: AC-3 simply enforces local consistency. Thus, it cannot guarantee that there are not global inconsistencies. 3.2.5 Approach 5 (Aya): Genetic Algorithm(GA) Reference: Holland, J.G.(1975), Adaptation in Nature and Artificial Systems. Review of "Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems by John H. Holland", The U. of Michigan Press, 1975 Reference: Mitchell, M. (1998), An Introduction to Genetic Algorithms. https://books.google.com.eg/books/about/An_Introduction_to_Genetic_Algorithms.html?id=0eznlz0TF-IC&redir_esc=y Classification: Papers in Evolutionary Algorithms and Meta-heuristics. Overview and Context: GAs is a reproduction of the process of natural selection. Their application to Graph Colouring involves the holding of a group of potential solutions, their growth through the methods of selection, crossover, and mutation, and the reduction of conflicts as the end result. This method is suitable for large graphs where the exhaustive search method is not an option due to the time involved. Algorithm Description: 1. Create different colourings consisted of random population. 2. Determine the fitness (number of conflicts). 3. Pick parents and perform crossover and mutation. 4. Get rid of the least fit individuals. 5. Continue till there is a conflict-free coloring or the maximum number of generations is reached. Pseudocode: def genetic_algorithm(max_generations, population): generation = 0 while generation < max_generations: fitness = evaluate_population(population) parents = select_parents(population, fitness) offspring = crossover_and_mutate(parents) population = replace_least_fit(population, offspring) if any(f == 0 for f in fitness): return population[fitness.index(0)] generation += 1 return None Experimental Setup & Results: Medium sized networks got tested working color patterns showed up after 50 to 500 rounds. Bigger groups or faster mutation shifts changed how quick and good the answers came out. Critical Analysis: Strengths: Can work with large graphs, versatile, can be done in parallel. Limitations: Parameters can have effects on the outcomes, may take a while in determining local optima, results not accurate. 3.2.6 Approach 6 (Aya): Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) Reference: Dorigo, M , & Stützle, T. (2004). Ant colony optimization. Classification: Swarm Intelligence / Metaheuristic Overview and Context: ACO is an algorithm that is taken from the natural behavior of ants. Artificial ants, through the use of pheromones and heuristics, are able to create vertex coloring. The algorithm is considered strong in large CSPs and in imperious graphs. Algorithm Description: 1. The pheromones are initialized on vertex color pairs. 2. Ants construct solutions based on probability. 3. The fitness (conflicts) is evaluated. 4. Pheromones are updated: good solutions are strengthened, and others are evaporated. 5. It is repeated until a valid coloring is obtained or the maximum number of iterations is reached. Pseudocode: def ant_colony_optimization(max_iterations, ants): pheromones = initialize_pheromones() for _ in range(max_iterations): solutions = [] for _ in range(ants): sol = construct_solution(pheromones) fit = evaluate_fitness(sol) solutions.append((sol, fit) pheromones = update_pheromones(pheromones, solutions) for sol, fit in solutions: if fit == 0: Experimental Setup and Results: The experiments were performed on DIMACS and random graphs. The method was able to find valid colorings in tens to hundreds of iterations. The method was not affected by the local optima problem. Critical Analysis: Strengths: The algorithm's capability of searching a vast area, and its execution in parallel remain its most significant advantages. Limitations: Results are highly dependent on parameter settings and sometimes even minor graphs consume a lot of time, hence the need for Heuristic rule has arisen as a result. 3.2.7 Approach 7 (Tibah): Tabu Search (TS) Reference: Hossein-Mohand, H., Hossein-Mohand, H., Albanese, V., & Olmos Gómez, M. del C. Furthermore, movement between neighboring solutions is achieved by recoloring nodes - to get out of the looping derivation of the same dump table and skip local optimization for the perfect balance of exploration and exploitation - which ultimately empowers better solutions. Algorithm Description The tabu search for usable initial solutions, then seeks and recognizes alternative solutions. It can accept or reject moves based on tabu and aspiration measures, and exchanges of elements based on proven records can assist in solution finding. These include the level of taboo, candidate range and aspiration interest. (2020).. Classification: Foundational concept, New to GCP| Meta-heuristic, stochastic local search. Overview and Context Simulated Annealing (SA) is a solution to NP-complete Graph Coloring Problem because SA probabilistically accepts a "worse" solution and since every state can be treated as some graph coloring (not a cost function like the other solutions explored thus far) (Besta et al., 2020). Moreover, since SA is a cooling agent to cool down its temperature of randomness, exploration and quality of solution/time efficiency can also be explored. Algorithm Description Simulated Annealing is a bottom-up approach from a base case and colors based on cost function which is the number of conflicts. Simulated Annealing looks at one vertex from a selection randomly attempting to recolor it. It creates neighbors around one vertex in a graph and then over time, it accepts better solutions and probabilistically worse solutions as it cools down the temperature coefficients over time which cools down the randomness and stabilizes (zero conflicts). Pseudocode Initialize coloring Set initial temperature while temperature > minimum do Select a vertex to recolor Evaluate new conflicts Accept better or probabilistically worse coloring Update best coloring found Cool temperature end return best coloring Experimental Setup Simulated Annealing was empirically evaluated through multi-core server conditions with plenty of real and synthetic graphs that are large (Besta et al., 2020). Smoothed annealed graphs with different temperatures, different cooling patterns, different amounts of iterations. Different resultant amounts of colors, conflicts, time taken, relative success in large challenges compared to Greedy heuristics. Compared to internal hill climbing solutions relative to the paper for additional comparison/control graphs, parallel graph-coloring approaches, etc. Reported Results SA found higher quality colors produced than greedy but took longer to generate. Scaled down findings worked better in a parallel system than Simulated Annealing (too sensitive to be cooling schedule) but Simulated Annealing can escape local minimum accepting probabilistically higher amounts of conflicts. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Simulated Annealing works wonder when enough time is taken for everything explored; it escapes local minima with no issues and finds solutions with good quality. However, it is sensitive to parameters and moderately scalable as compared to parallel efforts which don't scale practically (but are more successful) so it's successful in moderately sized systems when quality GCPs are looking for. Classification: [Recent] [Category: Heuristic/Meta-heuristic (learning-based)] Overview and Context The Graph neural network approach is a deep learning algorithm that learns from data that is graph structured. what differentiate it from other neural networks is that it works on relations between two connected nodes. The algorithm it self was firstly introduced in 2017 and used for the graph coloring diagram specifically 2020 (Li et al., 2022). Algorithm Description The algorithm works on learning nodes through iterative information sent between connected nodes. The nodes start with an initial vector and updates it by collecting information from the other nodes connected to it. This process is called ‘message passing’, the process continues to repeat itself until it forms several layers of information then a prediction layer is added to reduce errors and assigns outputs. Figure 6 Pseudocode Require: G = (V, E, p) Ensure: Assignment of colors c : V → Z1 1: next ← ∅, prev ← ∅ 2: parallel for u ∈ V 3: pred(u) ← v ∈ N (u) : p(v) > p(u) 4: succ(u) ← v ∈ N (u) : p(u) > p(v) 5: count(u) ← |pred(u)| 6: if count(u) = 0 7: atomic prev ← prev + {u} 8: 9: while prev̸ = ∅ 10: parallel for u ∈ prev 11: c(u) ← min color among pred(u) 12: for v ∈ succ(u) 13: atomic count(v) ← count(v) – 1 14 : if count(v) = 0 15: atomic next ← next + {v} 16: swap(next, prev) Experimental Setup 1- Datasets: • 5,158 nodes, 641,202 edges, chromatic number fixed at 3 • Includes classic test cases like queen, myciel, games, insertions 2- Parameter Settings • Before processing Remove nodes with degree < k. • After processing Local improvements • Iteration limit is 1000 iterations or 24 hours of running 3- Evaluation Metrics • Solved ratio: 1 − (#conflicts / #edges) • Fixed color ratio: Ability to respect pre-color constraints. • Cost: Number of errors in coloring result. • Runtime: Execution time 4- Baseline Methods • Tabucol (meta-heuristic). • HybridEA (meta-heuristic). Foundational exact methods like Backtracking and DSATUR (Brelaz, 1979) are optimal, yet they have a weakness like exponential complexity. Modern exact variants employing Branch-and-Bound (San Segundo et al., 2016) shrink the search space because the use bounding techniques, which is resulting in quantifiable performance gains but with the same scalability limitations. On the other hand, meta-heuristics like Genetic Algorithms, ACO, Tabu Search, and Simulated Annealing basically prioritize runtime efficiency and effectiveness and solution quality over optimality. All these algorithms keep outperforming the exact solvers on large graphs. TS and ACO show a strong ability to escape local minima, while GA and SA provide greater tunability but with a weakness in parameter sensitivity. Now the latest and newest research include the Hybrid and learning-based approaches. The cultural algorithms provide a proper balance between the speed and robustness. Graph Neutral Networks are the most scalable, which learn generalizable heuristics that perform better than classical meta-heuristics on several datasets, especially when GPU acceleration is used. 4 Critical Analysis and Discussion 4.1 Performance Comparison and Trade-offs 4.1 Performance Comparison and Trade-offs Exact approaches, including Backtracking/DSATUR (Brélaz, 1979 [4]) and the enhanced Branch-and-Bound solver (San Segundo et al., 2016 [5]), identify the most optimal colourings but are unable to ensure scalability due to their exponential time for large graphs. Exact methods are best applied to small and medium-sized graphs that are dense and have optimality as a priority. Heuristic approaches based on constraints (MRV + Forward Checking (Frost & Dechter, 1994 [6]) and AC-3 (Kalandaragh, 2022 [7])) establish solutions quickly by representing solutions in a pruned space. MRV + FC is useful when early failures exist, while AC-3 works better under tighter constraints; however, it quickly becomes expensive when constraints must be revised across many arcs. Meta-heuristic approaches are more scalable. Genetic Algorithms (Holland, 1975 [8]; Mitchell, 1998 [9]) and ACO (Dorigo & Stützle, 2004 [10]) exhibit improvements with very large graphs, allowing for a solution without searching through every option; however, careful tuning of parameters is required. Tabu Search (Hossein-Mohand et al., 2025 [11]) has the most consistency in performance because of the diversified methods based on memory, while Simulated Annealing (Besta et al., 2020 [12]) finds high-quality solutions but is sensitive to cooling methods and setup. Hybrid approaches and learning-based approaches GNN models (Li et al., 2022 [13]; Langedal & Manne, 2025 [14]) and Cultural Algorithms (Abbasian et al., 2011 [15]; Basmassi & Mouhoub, 2020 [16]) appear to have the most scalability and adaptability. GNNs do an efficient job at minimizing conflicts but depend heavily on training data and computational resources. Tradeoffs exist across various methods: • Exact approaches = accuracy, poor scalability • Constraint based approaches = efficiency, limited depth • Meta heuristic = scalability, sensitive to parameters • Learning based = high adaptability, costly computational costs. Then, we had improved exact methods [5] that employed stronger probing and bounds. From the mid-1990s on, literature began to shift toward meta-heuristics—GA [8], [9], SA [12], ACO [10], TS [11] being developed, which sought to avoid the constraints of scalability through stochastic exploratory methods rather than exhaustive reasoning. Recent trends (2020–2025) have been developed on hybrid approaches and learning-based optimization. For example, constraint propagation such as AC-3 [7] is used within larger solvers; Cultural Algorithms [15], [16] combine knowledge and evolutionary search; and GNNs learn heuristics directly from the data. Evidently, the approach is shifting towards an adaptive, data-led approach that goes beyond graphs. 4.2 Backtracking pseudocode (you can paste this)

text
procedure BACKTRACK_COLOR(G, k):
    n ← number of vertices in G
    color[0..n-1] ← 0              // 0 = unassigned
    domain[v] ← {1..k} for all v   // available colors for each vertex

    if BACKTRACK(0):
        return color
    else:
        return "No k-coloring exists"

procedure BACKTRACK(depth):
    if all vertices are colored:
        return true

    v ← SELECT_UNCOLORED_VERTEX()          // MRV or DSATUR-based

    for each c in domain[v]:               // try each available color
        if IS_CONSISTENT(v, c):
            assigned[v] ← true
            color[v] ← c

            // Forward Checking: temporarily prune neighbors’ domains
            pruned ← []
            for each neighbor u of v such that not assigned[u]:
                if c in domain[u]:
                    remove c from domain[u]
                    add (u, c) to pruned
                    if domain[u] is empty:
                        // undo pruning and backtrack
                        UNDO_PRUNING(pruned)
                        assigned[v] ← false
                        color[v] ← 0
                        goto NEXT_COLOR

            if BACKTRACK(depth + 1):
                return true

            // undo FC when backtracking
            UNDO_PRUNING(pruned)
            assigned[v] ← false
            color[v] ← 0

    NEXT_COLOR:
    return false

You can define SELECT_UNCOLORED_VERTEX() as:

text
function SELECT_UNCOLORED_VERTEX():
    // MRV: choose vertex with smallest domain size
    best ← null
    best_size ← +∞
    for each vertex v with assigned[v] = false:
        if size(domain[v]) < best_size:
            best_size ← size(domain[v])
            best ← v
    return best

5.1 Solution encoding

5.2 Belief space structure

Our belief space stores:

  • Normative knowledge: for each vertex, a set of preferred colors learned from the best individuals in the current generation.

  • Situational knowledge: the best individual discovered so far.
    This knowledge then influences how new candidates are generated and mutated.

5.3 Algorithm workflow (high-level)

  1. Initialize belief space (no preferences or random)

  2. Generate initial population of random colorings

  3. Evaluate each individual (count conflicts)

  4. Select best individuals → update belief space

  5. Generate new population influenced by belief space

  6. Repeat until:

    • max generations OR

    • conflict-free coloring (fitness = 0)

5.4 Cultural Algorithm pseudocode (you can paste)

text
procedure CULTURAL_GCP(G, k, pop_size, max_gen):
    POP ← INITIALIZE_POPULATION(pop_size, G, k)
    BELIEF ← INITIALIZE_BELIEF(G, k)

    BEST ← argmin_{ind ∈ POP} fitness(ind)

    gen ← 0
    while gen < max_gen and fitness(BEST) > 0:
        // 1. Acceptance: choose elite individuals
        ELITE ← SELECT_ELITE(POP)

        // 2. Update belief space based on ELITE
        UPDATE_BELIEF(BELIEF, ELITE)

        // 3. Influence: create new population guided by BELIEF
        NEW_POP ← []
        while size(NEW_POP) < pop_size:
            p1, p2 ← SELECT_PARENTS(ELITE)
            child ← CROSSOVER(p1, p2)
            child ← MUTATE_WITH_BELIEF(child, BELIEF)
            NEW_POP.append(child)

        POP ← NEW_POP
        current_best ← argmin_{ind ∈ POP} fitness(ind)
        if fitness(current_best) < fitness(BEST):
            BEST ← current_best

        gen ← gen + 1

    return BEST

Key functions you define in text:

  • fitness(ind): counts how many edges (u, v) have color[u] = color[v]

  • SELECT_ELITE(POP): pick top X% with lowest conflicts

  • UPDATE_BELIEF(BELIEF, ELITE): for each vertex, increase preference for colors used by elite

  • MUTATE_WITH_BELIEF(child, BELIEF):

    • pick a random vertex v

    • with some probability p_belief, assign a color from its preferred set; else random color

import time

def timed_run(solver_func, *args, **kwargs):
    start = time.time()
    result = solver_func(*args, **kwargs)
    end = time.time()
    elapsed_ms = (end - start) * 1000
    return result, elapsed_ms

    • chooses the first uncolored vertex

Skeleton:

python
def solve_backtracking_basic(adj, k):
    n = len(adj)
    color = [0] * n

    def is_safe(v, c):
        for u in adj[v]:
            if color[u] == c:
                return False
        return True

    def backtrack(v):
        if v == n:
            return True
        if color[v] != 0:
            return backtrack(v + 1)
        for c in range(1, k + 1):
            if is_safe(v, c):
                color[v] = c
                if backtrack(v + 1):
                    return True
                color[v] = 0
        return False

    success = backtrack(0)
    return color if success else None

Test it with small n (e.g. 5–8).

Dependency: Phase 1 utilities ready.
This step gives you something correct early, even if slow.

python
def solve_cultural_basic(adj, k, pop_size=50, max_gen=200):
    n = len(adj)
    population = [random_coloring(n, k) for _ in range(pop_size)]

    def select_elite(pop, elite_ratio=0.2):
        scored = [(fitness(adj, ind), ind) for ind in pop]
        scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
        elite_count = max(1, int(elite_ratio * len(pop)))
        return [ind for (_, ind) in scored[:elite_count]]

    # simple crossover & mutation...

No belief space yet – just evolution.

Instead of pure random mutation:

python
def mutate_with_belief(child, belief, k, mutation_rate=0.1):
    n = len(child)
    for v in range(n):
        if random.random() < mutation_rate:
            # 50% choose from preferred, 50% random
            preferred = list(belief["preferred_colors"][v])
            if preferred and random.random() < 0.7:
                child[v] = random.choice(preferred)
            else:
                child[v] = random.randint(1, k)
    return child

    python
    import random
import time

def generate_random_graph(n, density):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            from random import random as rnd
            if rnd() < density:
                adj[i].append(j)
                adj[j].append(i)
    return adj

def count_conflicts(adj, coloring):
    conflicts = 0
    for u in range(len(adj)):
        for v in adj[u]:
            if u < v and coloring[u] != 0 and coloring[u] == coloring[v]:
                conflicts += 1
    return conflicts

  3. Add a simple timed_run helper:

    python
    def timed_run(func, *args, **kwargs):
    start = time.time()
    result = func(*args, **kwargs)
    end = time.time()
    return result, (end - start) * 1000

  4. Commit: Add graph utilities and timing helper

  5. Push branch.
