Wrote the Introduction (Section 2), including Problem Statement (2.1), Motivation and Significance (2.2), and Scope of Review (2.3). 1. Abstract and Keywords 1.1 Abstract The Graph Coloring Problem is a conventional optimization problem in NP-hard class with relevant applications in resource management in networks, scheduling, register allocation, and frequency assignment. This paper presents an overview of the ten major algorithmic categories of approaches to solve the GCP problem including learning-based optimization, heuristic search, and meta-heuristic search, plus exact algorithms. Classical methods are addressed such as Branch-and-Bound and Backtracking/DSATUR together with constraint-driven heuristics including Minimum Remaining Values with Forward Checking and meta-heuristics that included Genetic Algorithms, Ant Colony Optimization, and Tabu Search. There is a trade-off between optimality and scalability that is clear from the literature. Exact methods guarantee optimality but have an exponential runtime. Meta-heuristic and hybrid modeling methods are returning faster, near-optimal solutions on difficult and large graphs. Learning-based methods demonstrated rapid scalability and adaptability. This work compares knowledge-guided evolutionary computation to a deterministic search through a Backtracking Search Algorithm and a Cultural Algorithm. This group specifically shows how the more recent literature on graph coloring is beginning to shift towards adaptive, data-driven optimization. Keywords Graph Coloring Problem, Backtracking Search, DSATUR, Meta-heuristics, Cultural Algorithms 2. Introduction 2.1 Problem Statement The Graph Coloring Problem has been a challenge in graph theory for a long time. A set of to circled colors assigned to the vertices of a graph where no 2 same-colored vertices are connected to each other with a line while using the least amount of colors possible. The number of total colors used is known as (Chromatic Number). The determination of the least amount of colors possible is an NP problem "nondeterministic polynomial-time" (the proposed solution can be verified quickly but for which finding the solution may be very slow). This means that there is no particular algorithm is optimal for the coloring graph, as the size of the graph increases the number of colored vertices combinations increases exponentially. There is other alternatives as backtracking, branch-and-bound, and integer programming can be useful but all of the when it comes to efficiency they lack it (Lewis & Palmer, 2025) . Therefore the graph coloring challenge has become a benchmark for algorithms optimization recent studies continued to emphasize the relevance of this problem (Lewis & Palmer, 2025). The focus of this paper is to try to propose solutions using AI algorithms to make coloring graphs better. The research goal is to show how AI algorithms can be a great solutions for the graph coloring problem. 2.2 Motivation and Significance The Graph Coloring Problem is significant because it shows real world optimization problems that require no obstacles with allocation while having limited resources. For example, in wireless networks, frequencies assigned to transmitters must avoid clashing with one another exactly like vertex coloring, no color should interfere with itself. According to IEEE survey in 2025 over 70% of spectrum management algorithms in 5G networks use graph based networks (Dai et al., 2025). Showing that graphs have significant importance to everyday uses. Also in timetabling and scheduling have concepts that rely on the same idea of coloring graphs that no tasks interfere with each other in the same time, the time here acts as the colored vertex. Beyond its uses, graph coloring stays one of the most enduring NP problems in algorithmic studies, it has great challenges in scalability and adaptability. Traditional non AI algorithms fails to effectively solve large graphs. Recent research shows that the potential of AI and metaheuristic algorithms is better to achieve faster and optimal results (Karaboğa & Kaya, 2024). Solving graph coloring through AI not only makes the understanding of optimization better but also gives benefits for industries that rely on the same theme or idea of graph coloring 2.3 Scope of This Review The research focuses on emphasizing how AI can serve the purpose of improving the graph coloring it examines both seminal works from the 2000s and the 1900s and recent research papers from the 2020s period. Those research papers show how AI can improve the algorithm. However this research does not focus purely on graph coloring proofs but it also focuses on algorithms with AI based optimization. 3. Literature Review 3.1 Overview and Classification of Approaches The approaches our group picked can be divided or classified into four main categories: exact algorithms, constraint- based heuristics, meta-heuristic methods, and hybrid or learning-based models. Exact methods give us optimal colorings through the pruning and systematic exploration. They are only suitable for smaller graphs since they have limitations by exponential time complexity. On the bright side, they are highly accurate. Constraint-based heuristics make the classical backtracking better and more improved by picking the most constrained variables first and reducing domains early. Works well and effectively for medium-sized constraint networks, since they are lightweight. Meta-heuristic approaches are optimal and scalable. They use randomness and adaptive memory, or swarm behavior to escape local minima. They are good for larger graphs. Lastly, hybrid and learning-based models incorporate knowledge-driven behavior and learned heuristics. They are scalable and robust, and work good for large and complex graph instances. 3.2 Detailed Review of Selected Approaches 3.2.1 Approach 1(Salma): Backtracking/ Depth-First Search Reference: Brélaz, D. (1979). New methods to color the vertices of a graph. Communications of the ACM, 22(4), 251–256. https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/359094.359101 Classification: Foundational / Exact Overview and Context In 1979, Brélaz introduced the Degree of Saturation (DSATUR) algorithm, a depth-first backtracking heuristic for the Graph Colouring Problem (GCP). GCP seeks the minimum number of colours to be used by which adjacent vertices are differently coloured. Brélaz proposed a heuristic method to order the vertices with the aim of reducing the search space since the problem was NP-complete. The majority of heuristic and exact coloring algorithms were built on top of DSATUR. Algorithm Description Algorithm Description DSATUR dynamically chooses the vertex that is not colored with the highest saturation degree, which basically is the number of different colors among its colored neighbors. Ties are broken by vertex degree. The saturation degree values of its neighbors are updated, and the selected vertex is given the smallest possible color. Backtracking occurs only when there is no legal color available in order to effectively prune the search tree (Brélaz, 1979). Figure 1 [4] This is a graph example that Brelaz (1979) used to demonstrate DSATUR coloring Pseudocode (adapted from Brélaz (1979)) Input: Graph G(V,E) Output: Valid coloring 1. Order vertices by decreasing degree. 2. Color the first vertex with colour 1. 3. While uncolored vertices remain: a. Select vertex v with maximum saturation degree.  b. Assign v the smallest permissible colour.  c. Update neighbours’ saturation degrees.Return colouring Experimental Setup(from the paper) It was compared to Welsh-Powell (1967), Matula et al. (1972), Dunstan (1975), and Tehrani (1975) on 55 randomly generated graphs of densities between 0.26 and 0.82. CPU time and color count were also in the metrics. Reported Results DSATUR obtained near-optimal solutions (<2 % deviation) and was computationally more efficient than earlier heuristics. it was precise and true for bipartite graphs. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Simple, efficient, and eﬀective for dense graphs; forms a foundation of many modern exact coloring algorithms. Limitations: non-parallel structure; worse performance on sparse or large graphs; exponential worst-case complexity. 3.2.2 Approach 2 (Salma): Brand and Bound (New DSATUR-Based Exact Algorithm) Reference: San Segundo, P., Rodríguez-Losada, D., & Jiménez, A. (2016). A new DSATUR-based algorithm for exact vertex coloring. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0305054811002966?via%3Dihub Classification: Recent / Exact (Branch-and-Bound Algorithm) Overview and Context In this paper, San Segundo et al. (2016) revisit Brélaz's (1979) DSATUR framework to develop a modern B&B exact solver for GCP. Recognizing the inefficiency of DSATUR's backtracking search on large graphs, the authors introduce tighter bounding rules, faster data structures, and a design suitable for parallelization. Their objective was to preserve DSATUR's user-friendly saturation-based logic while creating an exact solver that matched or outperformed commercial tools. Algorithm Description The technique incorporates the dynamic vertex ordering of DSATUR into a B&B structure. Each node represents a partial coloring, where the branching is guided by saturation degree.While greedy colorings maintain upper bounds on the chromatic number, maximal cliques give lower bounds. Whenever partial solutions surpass the best-known bound, branches are cut off. While incremental feasibility checks and compact color encoding further reduce computational overhead, a depth-first search ensures memory efficiency (San Segundo et al., 2016). Pseudocode (adapted from San Segundo et al., 2016) procedure COLOR(G, current_coloring, UB) if all vertices colored: UB ← min(UB, colors_used) return select vertex v with highest saturation degree for each feasible color c ≤ UB: assign(v, c) if colors_used + lower_bound(G, current_coloring) < UB: COLOR(G, current_coloring, UB) unassign(v) Experimental Setup(from the paper) The Benchmarks are: DIMACS COLOR02 suite (e.g., DSJC250.5, le450_25a). The Hardware: Intel Core i7 3.4 GHz, 16 GB RAM, single thread. Baselines include the traditional DSATUR, PASS, and B&C versions. Metrics include number of instances solved to optimality, node expansion, and execution time. Reported Results The new DSATUR-B&B solver, with an average speedup of 4× over classical DSATUR, 2× over PASS, reduced memory usage by half, while optimally coloring 62 out of 67 DIMACS instances. On a single core, it scaled to graphs with about 1000 vertices. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Ensures precise chromatic numbers; highly optimized implementation; significant runtime improvement through tight bounds and incremental updates. Limitations: Memory usage rises on dense graphs; worst-case time is still exponential; currently single-threaded without parallel execution. 3.2.3 Approach 3 (Alyaa): Constraint Satisfaction Heuristic (MRV + Forward Checking) Reference: D. Frost and R. Dechter, “In search of the best constraint satisfaction search,” in Proc. AAAI, Seattle, WA, USA, 1994, pp. 301–306. [6] https://www.aaai.org/Papers/AAAI/1994/AAAI94-046.pdf Classification: Foundational | Heuristic Search Overview and context The MRV + FC technique leverages the Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic and Forward Checking (FC) pruning in order to optimize backtracking search in constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), similar to Graph Coloring. MRV + FC operates on the idea of making the "hardest" choice first (MRV) and being able to quickly prune conflicts (FC) in order to reduce the size of the search tree. Recent work [17] examines the impact of propagation (the domain reductions created by FC) in both dynamic heuristics [17] in general. Algorithm Description The MRV + FC method works as a variable-ordering and lookahead technique. • MRV (Variable Ordering): MRV selects the unassigned variable with the fewest remaining values. Taking a fail-first approach, the MRV variable is the variable that places sufficient restrictions on all values, thus increasing the likelihood of failure early on and reducing branching factor. • FC (Lookahead): After assigning a value to a variable, FC immediately propagates by removing that value from all directly adjacent neighbors (i.e. the unassigned values). This light propagation essentially guarantees at a minimum, local consistency will exist immediately and removes any breakages in consistency that would eventually lead to failure on later assignments. Pseudocode Experimental Setup (paraphrased from the papers) • Van der Marel et al. (2024) studied whether information flow (domain pruning like FC) yields dynamic heuristics in CSP search [17]. • Prestwich (2002) included FC into local search neighborhoods for graph coloring and evaluated them using geometric and equipartite graphs [18]. • Abuluaih et al. (2018) compared MRV+ as an improvement to MRV baseline on 10,000 Sudoku problems [19]. Reported Results Heuristics for the reduction of the domain drastically reduced searching effort compared to lexical ordering. Table 2 demonstrates that the median search nodes for heuristics for reduction of the domain were much less (439,935) than lexical ordering (2,775,788). This provides evidence of the principal lesson learned through MRV/FC: with domain information you can search better. • Improvement for Heuristics: Prestwich (2002) noted FC improved reduced coloring in local search neighborhoods [18]. • Reduction: MRV+ (2018) exhibited marked improvements in reducing recursive calls and backtrack during evaluation of the Sudoku benchmarks [19]. • Current Work: Our most recent work [17] substantiated propagation (FC or other) can be an effective navigational lead/guide for producing dynamic heuristics in search [17]. Critical Analysis Benefits: •Reduced Search Space: Highly powerful pruner because it facilitates fail-first approaches and discovers conflicts early on. •Light Overhead: FC is lightweight look-ahead providing quite favorable overhead versus benefit. •Composite Use: Integrates well into systematic backtracking and hybrid techniques. Weaknesses: •Weaker Pruner: FC reduces local consistency (it only uses direct neighbors) and therefore cannot discover inconsistencies further out like Arc Consistency. •Overhead Cost: Maintaining domains adds per node cost, and increased benefit is strongly based on problem structure and inconsistency level discovered. •Sensitive to Ties: Standard MRV performance is affected by ties in the MRV heuristic; therefore, developing rational tie-breaking strategies is crucial. 3.2.4 Approach 4 (Alyaa): Reference: Y. S. Kalandaragh, “Speeding up the Arc Consistency algorithm in Constraint Satisfaction Problems: A new modification of AC-3,” J. Algorithms Comput., vol. 54, no. 1, pp. 125–138, Jun. 2022. [7] Classification: Recent Paper (2020-2025) | Category: Exact Search Optimization Overview and Context Arc Consistency (AC)enforced through the AC-3 algorithms used to establish local consistency in CSPs by applying that every value in the domain of each variable is supported in the domains of its neighboring variables. This allows for strong domain pruning and for early detection of infeasibility. AC-3 is most used as a preprocessing step or to complement other methods, such as when implemented in a hybrid way in MAC. Recent work [7] is aimed at addressing the high computational burden of using AC-3. Algorithm Description AC-3 is a propagation algorithm driven by a queue: • Revision Loop: First, the algorithm builds a queue containing all of the constraint arcs in the CSP. • Pruning: The operation of REVISE(X, Y) removes any values from the domain of X that could not possibly be consistent with any value in the domain of Y. • Propagation: For each domain reduction, all incoming arcs are put back on the queue, allowing the propagation of any consistency revision until there are no more available revisions (i.e., the algorithm has reached a fixed point). Figure 3 Pseudocode Experimental Setup (for AC-3 Modification – Based on Kalandaragh 2022) In [7], the authors assess the modified AC-3 algorithm with a benchmark of traditional CSP datasets comprised of conventional graph-coloring problems and Radio Link Frequency Assignment Problems (RLFAP). The experiments look at the modified AC-3 against baseline AC-3 in terms of: • Domain reduction ratios (Tables 3 - 4) • Discriminability measurements (Table 5) • aggregates for checks for total consistency and implications for revises The evaluation included runs of AC-3 in stand-alone form and hybrids incorporating MAC (Maintaining Arc Consistency) measures to evaluate improvement in pruning depth and Reported Results AC methods create reliable pruning with improved problem structure: Pruning Validation: Tables 3 and 4 show strong correlations between problem variables and domain reductions, supporting prunability reliability. Discriminability Gain: Table 5 shows increasing consistency significantly increases mean discriminability (i.e., 1.757 to 4.014^{+} with RLFAP100). This supports stronger propagation creates a more informative search space. Efficiency & Hybrid Gains: Hybrid algorithms with an integrated MAC performed significantly better than previous research implementations for robust graph coloring. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Advantages: · Superior Pruning: Results in stronger inference than FC: greater domain reduction along with a deeper look at inconsistency. · Enhanced Search Quality: Effort-saving through high discriminability (Table 5) and resultant problem simplification produced efficiencies for later search. Disadvantages: · High Computational Cost: The revision process becomes time-consuming on a per-propagation-step basis compared to FC. · Cost-Benefit: There should be some payoff if the pruning returns cost to overhead; the tradeoff may be different for the structure of the problem. · Incomplete: AC-3 simply enforces local consistency. Thus, it cannot guarantee that there are not global inconsistencies. 3.2.5 Approach 5 (Aya): Genetic Algorithm(GA) Reference: Holland, J.G.(1975), Adaptation in Nature and Artificial Systems. Review of "Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems by John H. Holland", The U. of Michigan Press, 1975 Reference: Mitchell, M. (1998), An Introduction to Genetic Algorithms. https://books.google.com.eg/books/about/An_Introduction_to_Genetic_Algorithms.html?id=0eznlz0TF-IC&redir_esc=y Classification: Papers in Evolutionary Algorithms and Meta-heuristics. Overview and Context: GAs is a reproduction of the process of natural selection. Their application to Graph Colouring involves the holding of a group of potential solutions, their growth through the methods of selection, crossover, and mutation, and the reduction of conflicts as the end result. This method is suitable for large graphs where the exhaustive search method is not an option due to the time involved. Algorithm Description: 1. Create different colourings consisted of random population. 2. Determine the fitness (number of conflicts). 3. Pick parents and perform crossover and mutation. 4. Get rid of the least fit individuals. 5. Continue till there is a conflict-free coloring or the maximum number of generations is reached. Pseudocode: def genetic_algorithm(max_generations, population): generation = 0 while generation < max_generations: fitness = evaluate_population(population) parents = select_parents(population, fitness) offspring = crossover_and_mutate(parents) population = replace_least_fit(population, offspring) if any(f == 0 for f in fitness): return population[fitness.index(0)] generation += 1 return None Experimental Setup & Results: Medium sized networks got tested working color patterns showed up after 50 to 500 rounds. Bigger groups or faster mutation shifts changed how quick and good the answers came out. Critical Analysis: Strengths: Can work with large graphs, versatile, can be done in parallel. Limitations: Parameters can have effects on the outcomes, may take a while in determining local optima, results not accurate. 3.2.6 Approach 6 (Aya): Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) Reference: Dorigo, M , & Stützle, T. (2004). Ant colony optimization. Classification: Swarm Intelligence / Metaheuristic Overview and Context: ACO is an algorithm that is taken from the natural behavior of ants. Artificial ants, through the use of pheromones and heuristics, are able to create vertex coloring. The algorithm is considered strong in large CSPs and in imperious graphs. Algorithm Description: 1. The pheromones are initialized on vertex color pairs. 2. Ants construct solutions based on probability. 3. The fitness (conflicts) is evaluated. 4. Pheromones are updated: good solutions are strengthened, and others are evaporated. 5. It is repeated until a valid coloring is obtained or the maximum number of iterations is reached. Pseudocode: def ant_colony_optimization(max_iterations, ants): pheromones = initialize_pheromones() for _ in range(max_iterations): solutions = [] for _ in range(ants): sol = construct_solution(pheromones) fit = evaluate_fitness(sol) solutions.append((sol, fit) pheromones = update_pheromones(pheromones, solutions) for sol, fit in solutions: if fit == 0: Experimental Setup and Results: The experiments were performed on DIMACS and random graphs. The method was able to find valid colorings in tens to hundreds of iterations. The method was not affected by the local optima problem. Critical Analysis: Strengths: The algorithm's capability of searching a vast area, and its execution in parallel remain its most significant advantages. Limitations: Results are highly dependent on parameter settings and sometimes even minor graphs consume a lot of time, hence the need for Heuristic rule has arisen as a result. 3.2.7 Approach 7 (Tibah): Tabu Search (TS) Reference: Hossein-Mohand, H., Hossein-Mohand, H., Albanese, V., & Olmos Gómez, M. del C. (2025). Classification: Recent | Category: Meta-heuristic Overview and Context In essence, Tabu Search is a machine that guarantees optimization and solves increasingly better solutions (Hossein-Mohand et al., 2025). This is done through a research memory that recalls (empowers) similar situations which allow avoidance. Furthermore, movement between neighboring solutions is achieved by recoloring nodes - to get out of the looping derivation of the same dump table and skip local optimization for the perfect balance of exploration and exploitation - which ultimately empowers better solutions. Algorithm Description The tabu search for usable initial solutions, then seeks and recognizes alternative solutions. It can accept or reject moves based on tabu and aspiration measures, and exchanges of elements based on proven records can assist in solution finding. These include the level of taboo, candidate range and aspiration interest. Reported Results TS provides optimal coloring rapidly, produces few alternatives and has consistent stability of performance with adaptive memory development for stability accumulates, relative to balanced computational abilities, pass second-party analytical means. Experimental Setup The Ts of GCP model is based on a formulation process with shared structure and database (2025) (Hossein-Mohand et al., 2025). They monitored formulation development relative to the duration of valid tabu (from 5to 10) and candidate width of approx. ⅕|V|, levels of aspiration, use the number of colors, contrast and time for evaluation, the formulation was compared to greed and imitation. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations TS excels in steering clear of locally optimal solutions due to the adaptive memory used relative to similar standards and little reliance on configuration (Hossein-Mohand et al., 2025). However, it operates with a time application reliance on tabu length and network composition resulting in high computational costs.it is O(|E|) and extensive research is performed with a development focus which Hossein-Mohand et al. (2025) also do. Pseudocode Initialize solution S Set S_best while stopping conditions not met do Explore neighborhood Select best admissible move Update Tabu List and S_best If no admissible move then diversify end return S_best Figure 4 3.1.8 Approach 8 (Tibah): Simulated Annealing (SA) Reference: Besta, M., Carigiet, A., Vonarburg-Shmaria, Z., Janda, K., Gianinazzi, L., & Hoefler, T. (2020).. Classification: Foundational concept, New to GCP| Meta-heuristic, stochastic local search. Overview and Context Simulated Annealing (SA) is a solution to NP-complete Graph Coloring Problem because SA probabilistically accepts a "worse" solution and since every state can be treated as some graph coloring (not a cost function like the other solutions explored thus far) (Besta et al., 2020). Moreover, since SA is a cooling agent to cool down its temperature of randomness, exploration and quality of solution/time efficiency can also be explored. Algorithm Description Simulated Annealing is a bottom-up approach from a base case and colors based on cost function which is the number of conflicts. Simulated Annealing looks at one vertex from a selection randomly attempting to recolor it. It creates neighbors around one vertex in a graph and then over time, it accepts better solutions and probabilistically worse solutions as it cools down the temperature coefficients over time which cools down the randomness and stabilizes (zero conflicts). Pseudocode Initialize coloring Set initial temperature while temperature > minimum do Select a vertex to recolor Evaluate new conflicts Accept better or probabilistically worse coloring Update best coloring found Cool temperature end return best coloring Experimental Setup Simulated Annealing was empirically evaluated through multi-core server conditions with plenty of real and synthetic graphs that are large (Besta et al., 2020). Smoothed annealed graphs with different temperatures, different cooling patterns, different amounts of iterations. Different resultant amounts of colors, conflicts, time taken, relative success in large challenges compared to Greedy heuristics. Compared to internal hill climbing solutions relative to the paper for additional comparison/control graphs, parallel graph-coloring approaches, etc. Reported Results SA found higher quality colors produced than greedy but took longer to generate. Scaled down findings worked better in a parallel system than Simulated Annealing (too sensitive to be cooling schedule) but Simulated Annealing can escape local minimum accepting probabilistically higher amounts of conflicts. Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Simulated Annealing works wonder when enough time is taken for everything explored; it escapes local minima with no issues and finds solutions with good quality. However, it is sensitive to parameters and moderately scalable as compared to parallel efforts which don't scale practically (but are more successful) so it's successful in moderately sized systems when quality GCPs are looking for. Figure 5 3.1.9 Approach 9 (Yousef): Graph Neutral Networks Based Coloring Reference: Li, W., Li, R., Ma, Y., Chan, S. O., Pan, D., & Yu, B. (2022) Reference: Langedal, K., & Manne, F. (2025). Classification: [Recent] [Category: Heuristic/Meta-heuristic (learning-based)] Overview and Context The Graph neural network approach is a deep learning algorithm that learns from data that is graph structured. what differentiate it from other neural networks is that it works on relations between two connected nodes. The algorithm it self was firstly introduced in 2017 and used for the graph coloring diagram specifically 2020 (Li et al., 2022). Algorithm Description The algorithm works on learning nodes through iterative information sent between connected nodes. The nodes start with an initial vector and updates it by collecting information from the other nodes connected to it. This process is called ‘message passing’, the process continues to repeat itself until it forms several layers of information then a prediction layer is added to reduce errors and assigns outputs. Figure 6 Pseudocode Require: G = (V, E, p) Ensure: Assignment of colors c : V → Z1 1: next ← ∅, prev ← ∅ 2: parallel for u ∈ V 3: pred(u) ← v ∈ N (u) : p(v) > p(u) 4: succ(u) ← v ∈ N (u) : p(u) > p(v) 5: count(u) ← |pred(u)| 6: if count(u) = 0 7: atomic prev ← prev + {u} 8: 9: while prev̸ = ∅ 10: parallel for u ∈ prev 11: c(u) ← min color among pred(u) 12: for v ∈ succ(u) 13: atomic count(v) ← count(v) – 1 14 : if count(v) = 0 15: atomic next ← next + {v} 16: swap(next, prev) Experimental Setup 1- Datasets: • 5,158 nodes, 641,202 edges, chromatic number fixed at 3 • Includes classic test cases like queen, myciel, games, insertions 2- Parameter Settings • Before processing Remove nodes with degree < k. • After processing Local improvements • Iteration limit is 1000 iterations or 24 hours of running 3- Evaluation Metrics • Solved ratio: 1 − (#conflicts / #edges) • Fixed color ratio: Ability to respect pre-color constraints. • Cost: Number of errors in coloring result. • Runtime: Execution time 4- Baseline Methods • Tabucol (meta-heuristic). • HybridEA (meta-heuristic). Figure (7) Reported Results: 1- Quantitative results: • GNN Achieved higher correct ratios across datasets more than TABUCOL and HYBIRDEA • GNN Solved 95% percent correctly rather than TABUCOL (85%) • GNN reduced conflicts compared to TABUCOL and HYBRIDEA. 2- Qualitative Findings • Scalability: GNN scaled better to larger graphs, while TABUCOL and HYBRIDEA struggled with runtime. • Stronger ability to respect fixed-color constraints compared to HYBRIDEA 3- Other methods • TABUCOL was nearly competitive but required long runtimes • HYBRIDEA gave good solutions but with high error rates Critical Analysis: Strengths and Limitations Graph neural networks has advantages by learning patterns from graphs, therefore making it easy to predict color patterns without certain rules. It can compute large datasets without needing much time or being expensive. Its downside is that if it faces an identifiable graph then it will have high risk of failure thus making it expensive. So as long as the graph is learned before it can solve it with ease. 3.1.10 Approach 10 (Yousef): Cultural Algorithm Reference: Abbasian, R., Mouhoub, M., & Jula, A. (2011). Reference: Basmassi, M. A., & Mouhoub, M. (2020). Classification: [Foundational] [Category: Hybird] Overview and Context The cultural algorithm was first introduced as an algorithm in 1994 by Robert G. Reynolds but was later on implemented on graph coloring by Ali, A. A., & Reynolds, R. G. (2008) (Abbasian, Mouhoub, & Jula, 2011). It was firstly made to enhance the search process and improve quality of solutions. Algorithm Description Cultural Algorithms mixes both learning and already known information allowing for faster performance and avoidance of local problems. It begins with a number of candidates then predicts conflicts to reduce them then the best solutions and learned patterns is stored in a ‘belief space’. The mix of knowledge and learning in this algorithm makes it near optimal. Figure (8) Pseudocode Begin Initialize the Belief space BLS(0) using Eq.3; Generate the initial population POP(0) using BLS(0); Evaluate POP(0); Repeat Select parents to be used by genetic operators; Generate new chromosomes using crossover; Applied mutation on the new chromosomes; Applied Hierarchical clustering to POP(t); correction; begin CH: New Chromosome. Palette[] <- Get all clusters of CH; /* divided clustering */ Repeat i from 0 to Palette[].lenght InSimilarity[i] <- Average Genes Evaluate POP(t); Acceptance (POP(t),BLS(t)); Update(BLS(t)); Influence (BLS(t),POP(t)); t <- t+1; Until (Terminating condition is reached); End; Figure (9) Experimental Setup 1- Dataset: Both research papers mentioned earlier used DIMACS (standard graph coloring instances. These are used in graph coloring to test algorithm performance (Basmassi & Mouhoub, 2020). 2- Parameters: 1- Implementation in java and python . 2- Population size, mutation rates, and clustering thresholds 3- Experiments run on a workstation with certain specs. 3- Evaluation Metrics: 1- Chromatic Number 2- Execution time 3- Robustness 4- Baseline Methods 1- DSATUR heuristic 2- Parallel Genetic-Tabu Algorithm Reported Results 1- Quantitative results 1- High chromatic numbers on DIMACS benchmark. 2- Lower operation times than classic heuristics. 3- Better scalability compared to other algorithms. 2- Qualitative findings 1- Stability 2- Robustness 3- Compared to other methods 1- Exceeded DSATUR in solution quality. 2- Similar or better stats than other metaheuristics in speed and accuracy. Critical Analysis This algorithm offers adaptability and conditioning based on the type of graph it encounters by combining knowledge and information stored in the belief space. Its power point is robustness and error avoidance. However, it is limited by its parameters like pc power, population size etc. This can limit its performance if the belief space information becomes biased. It does not guarantee the performance for huge graphs. 3.3 Comparative Summary Table 1: Comparative Summary of Reviewed Approaches Approach Year & Type Time Complexity Performance Scalability Reference Backtracking/ Depth-First Search 1979-Foundational/ Exact Exponential O(kⁿ) Near-optimal (< 2 % error) on dense graphs Limited (≤ 100 vertices) Brélaz (1979) Brand and Bound 2016 - Recent / Exact Exponential (reduced via bounding) Fast exact coloring; 4× speedup over classical DSATUR Scales to ≈ 1000 vertices San Segundo et al. (2016) Constraint Satisfaction Heuristics (MRV + Forward Checking) 1994 -Foundational Heuristic O(n·d²) typical Cuts many dead-ends; fewer node expansions Moderate Frost & Dechter (1994) Constraint Propagation (AC-3) 2022 - Recent Exact Search Optimization O(e·d³) Strong pruning; improves search quality; effective in hybrids Moderate Shokri Kalandaragh (2022) Genetic Algorithm(GA) 1975 -Foundational / Meta-Heuristic O(pop·gen·eval) Good solutions in 50–500 generations High Holland (1975) Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) 2004 -Foundational / Meta-Heuristic O(ants·iterations) Effective on dense and CSP-like graphs High Dorigo & Stützle (2004) Tabu Search (TS) 2025 - Recent / Meta-Heuristic O(|E|) per iteration Fast, stable, avoids local optima Moderate H. Hossein-Mohand et al. (2025) Simulated Annealing (SA) 2020 - Recent / Meta-Heuristic ≈ O(I × n) (iterations × vertices) Produces higher-quality colorings; longer runtime; escapes local minima Moderate Besta et al. (2020) Graph Neural Network (GNN) Based Coloring 2022-2025 - Recent / Learning-Based Heuristic Training: O(E × T); Inference: O(E) 95% solved ratio; fewer conflicts than Tabucol & HybridEA High – scales efficiently on large and dense graphs Li et al. (2022); Langedal & Manne (2025) Cultural Algorithms 2011 - 2020 - Foundational / Hybrid O(pop·gen·eval) Robust, good solution quality; strong hybrid performance Moderate–High Abbasian et al. (2011); Basmassi & Mouhoub (2020) The table above basically shows the evolution that happened from exact algorithms to meta-heuristic, hybrid, and learning-based approaches. Foundational exact methods like Backtracking and DSATUR (Brelaz, 1979) are optimal, yet they have a weakness like exponential complexity. Modern exact variants employing Branch-and-Bound (San Segundo et al., 2016) shrink the search space because the use bounding techniques, which is resulting in quantifiable performance gains but with the same scalability limitations. On the other hand, meta-heuristics like Genetic Algorithms, ACO, Tabu Search, and Simulated Annealing basically prioritize runtime efficiency and effectiveness and solution quality over optimality. All these algorithms keep outperforming the exact solvers on large graphs. TS and ACO show a strong ability to escape local minima, while GA and SA provide greater tunability but with a weakness in parameter sensitivity. Now the latest and newest research include the Hybrid and learning-based approaches. The cultural algorithms provide a proper balance between the speed and robustness. Graph Neutral Networks are the most scalable, which learn generalizable heuristics that perform better than classical meta-heuristics on several datasets, especially when GPU acceleration is used. 4 Critical Analysis and Discussion 4.1 Performance Comparison and Trade-offs 4.1 Performance Comparison and Trade-offs Exact approaches, including Backtracking/DSATUR (Brélaz, 1979 [4]) and the enhanced Branch-and-Bound solver (San Segundo et al., 2016 [5]), identify the most optimal colourings but are unable to ensure scalability due to their exponential time for large graphs. Exact methods are best applied to small and medium-sized graphs that are dense and have optimality as a priority. Heuristic approaches based on constraints (MRV + Forward Checking (Frost & Dechter, 1994 [6]) and AC-3 (Kalandaragh, 2022 [7])) establish solutions quickly by representing solutions in a pruned space. MRV + FC is useful when early failures exist, while AC-3 works better under tighter constraints; however, it quickly becomes expensive when constraints must be revised across many arcs. Meta-heuristic approaches are more scalable. Genetic Algorithms (Holland, 1975 [8]; Mitchell, 1998 [9]) and ACO (Dorigo & Stützle, 2004 [10]) exhibit improvements with very large graphs, allowing for a solution without searching through every option; however, careful tuning of parameters is required. Tabu Search (Hossein-Mohand et al., 2025 [11]) has the most consistency in performance because of the diversified methods based on memory, while Simulated Annealing (Besta et al., 2020 [12]) finds high-quality solutions but is sensitive to cooling methods and setup. Hybrid approaches and learning-based approaches GNN models (Li et al., 2022 [13]; Langedal & Manne, 2025 [14]) and Cultural Algorithms (Abbasian et al., 2011 [15]; Basmassi & Mouhoub, 2020 [16]) appear to have the most scalability and adaptability. GNNs do an efficient job at minimizing conflicts but depend heavily on training data and computational resources. Tradeoffs exist across various methods: • Exact approaches = accuracy, poor scalability • Constraint based approaches = efficiency, limited depth • Meta heuristic = scalability, sensitive to parameters • Learning based = high adaptability, costly computational costs. Figure (10) Figure (11) 4.2 Computational Complexity Analysis 5 Genetic Algorithm (GA) scales well to big graph colouring problems so does Ant Colony Optimization (ACO). While GA's runtime depends heavily on population size PPP, generation count GGG, also evaluation time per solution. We show its complexity this way: 6 O(P×G×cost(fitness)) 7 By mixing solutions randomly,GA checks lots of options quickly so it works well even on big or tight networks.ACO's trickiness relies on how many ants there are mmm, the rounds they go through ttt, also the effort it takes to build a coloring: 8 O(m×t×cost(construct_solution)) 9 Even though updating pheromones means more work at each step, ACO handles growth well while lowering chances of getting stuck in suboptimal spots. One doesn't outperform the other just by design success mostly depends on how you set the controls. 4.3 Evolution of Research: From Foundational to Current From Foundational to Current The domain began with deterministic search and intelligent ordering, such as DSATUR [4], that defined principles still being used today. Then, we had improved exact methods [5] that employed stronger probing and bounds. From the mid-1990s on, literature began to shift toward meta-heuristics—GA [8], [9], SA [12], ACO [10], TS [11] being developed, which sought to avoid the constraints of scalability through stochastic exploratory methods rather than exhaustive reasoning. Recent trends (2020–2025) have been developed on hybrid approaches and learning-based optimization. For example, constraint propagation such as AC-3 [7] is used within larger solvers; Cultural Algorithms [15], [16] combine knowledge and evolutionary search; and GNNs learn heuristics directly from the data. Evidently, the approach is shifting towards an adaptive, data-led approach that goes beyond graphs. Figure (12) 4.4 Practical Considerations GA’s easier to set up, though how well it runs depends on group size, changes during process, plus picking strategy. On the flip side, ACO needs careful tuning, especially how fast signals fade and importance of clues yet handles busy or tricky networks better. Most times, GA works great for quick tests; meanwhile, ACO shines when you need steady, reliable answers. 4.5 Identifies Gaps and Limitations From Foundational to Current The domain began with deterministic search and intelligent ordering, such as DSATUR [4], that defined principles still being used today. Then, we had improved exact methods [5] that employed stronger probing and bounds. From the mid-1990s on, literature began to shift toward meta-heuristics—GA [8], [9], SA [12], ACO [10], TS [11] being developed, which sought to avoid the constraints of scalability through stochastic exploratory methods rather than exhaustive reasoning. Recent trends (2020–2025) have been developed on hybrid approaches and learning-based optimization. For example, constraint propagation such as AC-3 [7] is used within larger solvers; Cultural Algorithms [15], [16] combine knowledge and evolutionary search; and GNNs learn heuristics directly from the data. Evidently, the approach is shifting towards an adaptive, data-led approach that goes beyond graphs. Figure (13) 4.6 Implications for Implementation (phase 2) In phase two, GA speeds up first tests while helping the team set basic performance markers. Yet ACO brings sharper tuning by boosting answers over time using trail-based feedback loops. Mixing both GA at start, ACO toward end delivers quicker outcomes plus stronger accuracy. Either approach adapts easily later, even as demands grow. Figure (14) 5 Conclusion This literature survey explored the Graph Coloring Problem and how it serves as an industrial solution frontrunner to optimization and AI search as a test bed for performance. Overall findings from the ten solutions surveyed suggest that exact solutions Backtracking and Branch-and-Bound are accurate and preferred at smaller problem sizes and that constraint-based heuristics are faster with higher degrees of localized optimized solutions. Similarly, meta-heuristic solutions GA, ACO, TS and SA provide equated benefits for larger and more diverse spaces but are also highly sensitive to predetermined parameters. Yet novel solutions, especially hybridized solutions and learning solutions - Cultural Algorithms and Graph Neural Networks provided the most flexible, scalable, and robust results for differently constrained graphs - demonstrates the industrial push for hybridized, data-driven, adaptive solutions that move beyond deterministic solutions with hybridized, data-driven, adaptive solutions with effective runtime efficiency. import random
import time

def generate_random_graph(n, density):
    """
    Generate an undirected random graph.

    n: number of vertices
    density: probability of edge between any pair (0..1)
    """
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if random.random() < density:
                adj[i].append(j)
                adj[j].append(i)
    return adj

def count_conflicts(adj, coloring):
    """
    Count number of conflicting edges for a given coloring.
    """
    conflicts = 0
    for u in range(len(adj)):
        for v in adj[u]:
            if u < v and coloring[u] == coloring[v]:
                conflicts += 1
    return conflicts

🧩 Step A — Import time & define helper structure

import time

Then replace your function with this skeleton:

python
import time

def solve_backtracking(adj, k, params=None):
    """
    Backtracking graph coloring with MRV + Forward Checking.
    adj: dict {node: [neighbors]}
    k:   number of colors
    """

    nodes = list(adj.keys())

    # metrics
    stats = {
        "nodes_explored": 0,
        "backtracks": 0,
    }

    # initial domains: every node can take any color 0..k-1
    domains = {v: set(range(k)) for v in nodes}
    assignment = {}  # node -> color

    start = time.perf_counter()

    success = _backtrack_recursive(adj, nodes, domains, assignment, stats)

    end = time.perf_counter()

    result = {
        "coloring": assignment if success else None,
        "nodes_explored": stats["nodes_explored"],
        "backtracks": stats["backtracks"],
        "time_ms": (end - start) * 1000.0,
    }
    return result

Now we need to write _backtrack_recursive and helpers.

🧠 Step B — Implement MRV choice

Add this function below solve_backtracking:

python
def _select_mrv_variable(nodes, domains, assignment, adj):
    """
    Choose the unassigned node with the smallest domain (MRV).
    Tie-break by highest degree.
    """
    unassigned = [v for v in nodes if v not in assignment]

    # MRV: smallest domain size
    best_v = None
    best_domain_size = None
    best_degree = None

    for v in unassigned:
        dsize = len(domains[v])
        degree = len(adj[v])
        if best_v is None or dsize < best_domain_size or (dsize == best_domain_size and degree > best_degree):
            best_v = v
            best_domain_size = dsize
            best_degree = degree

    return best_v

🔍 Step C — Consistency check

python
def _is_consistent(v, color, assignment, adj):
    """Check if assigning color to v violates any already-colored neighbor."""
    for neigh in adj[v]:
        if neigh in assignment and assignment[neigh] == color:
            return False
    return True

🔮 Step D — Forward Checking

python
def _forward_check(v, color, domains, assignment, adj):
    """
    Apply forward checking: remove 'color' from neighbors' domains.
    Return (ok, new_domains) where:
      ok = False if some neighbor domain becomes empty.
    """
    # copy domains (shallow copy of dict + sets)
    new_domains = {x: set(vals) for x, vals in domains.items()}

    for neigh in adj[v]:
        if neigh in assignment:
            continue
        if color in new_domains[neigh]:
            new_domains[neigh].remove(color)
            if len(new_domains[neigh]) == 0:
                return False, domains  # fail, keep old domains
    return True, new_domains

🔁 Step E — Recursive backtracking function

python
def _backtrack_recursive(adj, nodes, domains, assignment, stats):
    # if all nodes assigned → success
    if len(assignment) == len(nodes):
        return True

    stats["nodes_explored"] += 1

    # choose variable by MRV
    v = _select_mrv_variable(nodes, domains, assignment, adj)
    if v is None:
        return False

    # try colors in domain
    for color in list(domains[v]):
        if not _is_consistent(v, color, assignment, adj):
            continue

        # tentatively assign
        assignment[v] = color

        ok, new_domains = _forward_check(v, color, domains, assignment, adj)
        if not ok:
            stats["backtracks"] += 1
            del assignment[v]
            continue

        # recurse
        if _backtrack_recursive(adj, nodes, new_domains, assignment, stats):
            return True

        # undo assignment
        stats["backtracks"] += 1
        del assignment[v]

    return False

Now you have a full working backtracking solver with:

  • MRV

  • forward checking

  • metrics

python
import time

def solve_backtracking(adj, k, params=None):
    n = len(adj)
    colors = [-1] * n
    nodes_explored = 0
    backtracks = 0

    def is_safe(node, color):
        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == color:
                return False
        return True

    def backtrack(node):
        nonlocal nodes_explored, backtracks

        if node == n:
            return True

        nodes_explored += 1

        for color in range(k):
            if is_safe(node, color):
                colors[node] = color
                if backtrack(node + 1):
                    return True
                colors[node] = -1  # undo
                backtracks += 1

        return False

    t0 = time.time()
    success = backtrack(0)
    t1 = time.time()

    if not success:
        return {
            "coloring": None,
            "nodes_explored": nodes_explored,
            "backtracks": backtracks,
            "time_ms": (t1 - t0) * 1000,
        }

    return {
        "coloring": {i: colors[i] for i in range(n)},
        "nodes_explored": nodes_explored,
        "backtracks": backtracks,
        "time_ms": (t1 - t0) * 1000,
    }

🟦 STEP 2 — Upgrade to Backtracking + MRV

🔍 What changes conceptually?

  • Before: recursion used node index (0,1,2,..) in order.

  • Now: at each step we choose the uncolored vertex that has the fewest legal colors left → MRV.

So the recursion becomes:

  1. If all vertices colored → done.

  2. Build a list of all uncolored nodes.

  3. For each uncolored node, count how many colors are still allowed.

  4. Pick the one with minimum count = MRV node.

  5. Try colors for that node.

python
import time


def solve_backtracking(adj, k, params=None):
    """
    Backtracking graph coloring with MRV (Minimum Remaining Values) heuristic.

    adj : dict[int, list[int]]
        Adjacency list for graph, nodes are 0 .. n-1
    k   : int
        Maximum number of colors allowed (0 .. k-1)

    Returns a dictionary:
        {
            "coloring": {node: color} or None if no solution,
            "nodes_explored": int,
            "backtracks": int,
            "time_ms": float
        }
    """
    n = len(adj)
    colors = [-1] * n  # -1 = uncolored

    nodes_explored = 0
    backtracks = 0

    def is_safe(node, color):
        """Check if we can assign this color to this node."""
        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == color:
                return False
        return True

    def select_mrv_node():
        """
        Select the next node to color using MRV:
        choose the uncolored node with the fewest legal colors.
        """
        best_node = None
        best_count = None

        for node in range(n):
            if colors[node] != -1:
                continue  # already colored

            # count legal colors for this node
            legal_count = 0
            for c in range(k):
                if is_safe(node, c):
                    legal_count += 1

            # if no legal colors -> immediate failure
            if legal_count == 0:
                return node, 0

            if best_count is None or legal_count < best_count:
                best_count = legal_count
                best_node = node

        return best_node, best_count

    def all_colored():
        return all(c != -1 for c in colors)

    def backtrack():
        nonlocal nodes_explored, backtracks

        # Base case
        if all_colored():
            return True

        nodes_explored += 1

        # Choose next variable with MRV
        node, legal_count = select_mrv_node()

        # If no legal colors for this node → dead end
        if legal_count == 0:
            backtracks += 1
            return False

        # Try all legal colors for that node
        for color in range(k):
            if is_safe(node, color):
                colors[node] = color
                if backtrack():
                    return True
                # undo assignment
                colors[node] = -1
                backtracks += 1

        return False

    t0 = time.time()
    success = backtrack()
    t1 = time.time()

    result = {
        "coloring": None,
        "nodes_explored": nodes_explored,
        "backtracks": backtracks,
        "time_ms": (t1 - t0) * 1000,
    }

    if success:
        result["coloring"] = {i: colors[i] for i in range(n)}

    return result

🔥 What FC Does

Before trying a color, FC:

  1. Looks at neighbors

  2. Removes that color from their domain

  3. Checks if any neighbor has no legal colors left

  4. If so → prune immediately (don’t waste time exploring)

This massively reduces recursion.

python
import time


def solve_backtracking(adj, k, params=None):
    """
    Backtracking graph coloring with MRV + Forward Checking.
    """

    n = len(adj)
    colors = [-1] * n  # -1 = uncolored

    # Domain for each node = all possible colors initially
    domains = {i: set(range(k)) for i in range(n)}

    nodes_explored = 0
    backtracks = 0

    def is_safe(node, color):
        """Check if we can assign this color to this node."""
        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == color:
                return False
        return True

    def select_mrv_node():
        """
        Select the uncolored node with the smallest domain size (MRV).
        """
        uncolored = [i for i in range(n) if colors[i] == -1]
        if not uncolored:
            return None

        # MRV = choose node with minimum domain size
        return min(uncolored, key=lambda node: len(domains[node]))

    def forward_check(node, color):
        """
        Apply forward checking after assigning a color.
        Remove `color` from domains of neighbors.
        If any neighbor domain becomes empty -> failure.
        Return: removed_values (to allow undo)
        """
        removed = {}

        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == -1 and color in domains[neigh]:
                domains[neigh].remove(color)
                removed.setdefault(neigh, []).append(color)

                # No available colors → fail early
                if len(domains[neigh]) == 0:
                    return None  # failure

        return removed  # success

    def undo_forward_check(removed):
        """Restore pruned domain values."""
        for node, vals in removed.items():
            for v in vals:
                domains[node].add(v)

    def backtrack():
        nonlocal nodes_explored, backtracks

        # Base case: solved
        if all(colors[i] != -1 for i in range(n]):
            return True

        nodes_explored += 1

        # Select variable using MRV
        node = select_mrv_node()

        # Try colors in the node domain
        for color in list(domains[node]):
            if is_safe(node, color):
                colors[node] = color

                # Forward checking
                removed = forward_check(node, color)

                if removed is not None:
                    if backtrack():
                        return True

                # Undo assignment
                colors[node] = -1

                # Undo domain pruning
                if removed is not None:
                    undo_forward_check(removed)

                backtracks += 1

        return False

    # Run
    t0 = time.time()
    success = backtrack()
    t1 = time.time()

    result = {
        "coloring": None,
        "nodes_explored": nodes_explored,
        "backtracks": backtracks,
        "time_ms": (t1 - t0) * 1000,
    }

    if success:
        result["coloring"] = {i: colors[i] for i in range(n)}

    return result

⭐ 4.1 Algorithm Description — Backtracking with MRV and Forward Checking

The Backtracking Search Algorithm is a systematic depth-first search method used to construct a valid graph coloring by incrementally assigning colors to vertices while respecting adjacency constraints. The naïve backtracking approach explores nodes in a fixed order and attempts all possible colors, resulting in extensive search and exponential branching. To improve performance and reduce unnecessary exploration, this project integrates two constraint-directed heuristics widely used in Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs): Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) and Forward Checking (FC).

Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) is a dynamic variable-ordering heuristic that selects, at each step, the vertex with the smallest number of legal color options remaining in its domain. This “fail-first” principle increases early detection of dead-end branches, reducing the depth and breadth of the search tree. MRV is particularly effective in graph coloring because the difficulty of coloring a node increases as its domain shrinks due to neighbors’ assignments.

Forward Checking (FC) is a look-ahead inference mechanism applied after assigning a color to a vertex. The FC procedure removes the chosen color from the domains of all uncolored adjacent nodes. If any neighbor’s domain becomes empty as a result, the branch is terminated immediately. This prevents exploring paths that are guaranteed to fail, significantly reducing backtracking operations.

The combination of Backtracking, MRV, and Forward Checking transforms the algorithm into a powerful CSP solver. MRV ensures intelligent ordering of variable selection, while FC provides proactive constraint propagation. These additions reduce the overall search space, increase pruning efficiency, and improve runtime for medium-sized graphs—without sacrificing correctness or completeness. This enhanced algorithm forms the primary “exact” baseline solver used for comparison with the Cultural Algorithm in Phase 2.

⭐ 4.2 Pseudocode for Backtracking with MRV + Forward Checking

The following pseudocode describes the full solution procedure implemented in this project. It follows the CSP formulation of graph coloring, where each vertex is a variable and colors represent domain values.

Pseudocode

pseudo
procedure SOLVE_BACKTRACKING(adj, k):
    n ← number of vertices
    colors[i] ← -1 for all i               // -1 means unassigned
    domains[i] ← {0,1,...,k-1} for all i   // initial full color domains

    start timer

    if BACKTRACK():
        return coloring, nodes_explored, backtracks, time_elapsed
    else:
        return failure


procedure BACKTRACK():
    if all vertices are assigned:
        return True

    nodes_explored++

    // -------- Variable Ordering: MRV --------
    node ← SELECT_MRV_NODE()

    // -------- Try all colors in domain --------
    for each color in domains[node]:
        if IS_SAFE(node, color):
            colors[node] ← color

            removed ← FORWARD_CHECK(node, color)

            if removed ≠ FAILURE:
                if BACKTRACK():
                    return True

            // undo assignment + domain pruning
            colors[node] ← -1
            UNDO_FORWARD_CHECK(removed)
            backtracks++

    return False


procedure SELECT_MRV_NODE():
    uncolored ← { i | colors[i] = -1 }
    return node from uncolored with the smallest domain size


procedure IS_SAFE(node, color):
    for each neighbor in adj[node]:
        if colors[neighbor] = color:
            return False
    return True


procedure FORWARD_CHECK(node, color):
    removed ← empty set

    for each neighbor in adj[node]:
        if colors[neighbor] = -1 AND color ∈ domains[neighbor]:
            remove color from domains[neighbor]
            record removal in removed

            if domains[neighbor] = empty:
                return FAILURE

    return removed


procedure UNDO_FORWARD_CHECK(removed):
    restore all removed domain values

4.3 Backtracking Algorithm Flowchart

This subsection presents the flow of our Backtracking-based Graph Coloring solver with the MRV (Minimum Remaining Values) heuristic and Forward Checking. The goal of the flowchart is to show how the algorithm:

  1. Starts from an uncolored graph

  2. Repeatedly chooses the most constrained vertex (MRV)

  3. Tries each legal color

  4. Uses Forward Checking to prune impossible colors for neighbors

  5. Either finds a full valid coloring or backtracks when a dead-end is reached.

4.3.1 Textual Explanation of the Flow

  1. Start

    • Initialize performance counters (nodes explored, backtracks, time).

    • Initialize colors dict with all vertices unassigned (e.g., -1).

  2. All Vertices Colored?

    • Check if every vertex has a color.

    • Yes → solution found → go to “Build Result and Return Success”.

    • No → continue.

  3. Select Next Vertex using MRV

    • Among uncolored vertices, compute the number of currently legal colors (given existing assignments).

    • Choose the vertex with the smallest number of legal colors (fail-first strategy).

    • If there is a tie, break using degree or simple index order.

  4. Compute Legal Colors for Selected Vertex

    • For each color c in {0, 1, …, k−1}:

      • Check if any already-colored neighbor uses c.

    • Collect into a list legal_colors.

  5. Any Legal Color Available?

    • If legal_colors is empty:

      • This is a dead-end for the current partial assignment.

      • Increase backtrack counter.

      • Return Failure to previous recursive call (backtrack).

  6. For Each Legal Color (Loop)

    • Assign the current vertex v the chosen color c.

    • Apply Forward Checking:

      • For each uncolored neighbor u of v, temporarily remove c from u’s domain.

      • If any neighbor’s domain becomes empty → this color choice leads to inconsistency.

  7. Domain Wipe-Out After Forward Checking?

    • If some neighbor now has no legal color:

      • Undo the FC changes and the assignment to v.

      • Move to the next color in legal_colors.

  8. Recursive Call

    • If domains are still consistent:

      • Recursively call backtracking on the updated partial assignment.

      • If the recursive call returns Success:

        • Propagate Success upward (no more search needed).

  9. Undo Assignment and FC (When Recursive Call Fails)

    • If recursion returns Failure:

      • Undo the color assignment to v.

      • Restore neighbors’ domains (reverse FC changes).

      • Try the next color for v.

  10. All Colors Tried and Failed?

    • If all colors in legal_colors have been tried and all lead to failure:

      • Increase backtrack counter.

      • Return Failure to the previous level.

  11. Build Result and Return Success

    • When all vertices are colored consistently:

      • Construct the result dictionary:

        • coloring (vertex → color)

        • nodes_explored

        • backtracks

        • time_ms

      • Return this result to the caller (e.g., main.py or GUI).

⭐ 4.4 Implementation Details (Backtracking Algorithm)

The Backtracking solver for the Graph Coloring Problem was implemented in Python following a Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) formulation. The algorithm assigns colors to vertices incrementally while enforcing adjacency constraints. To improve the efficiency of classical backtracking, two enhancements were integrated: Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) for dynamic variable ordering and Forward Checking (FC) for domain pruning.

The following subsections describe the key implementation components used in the solver.

4.4.1 Data Structures

Adjacency List (Graph Representation)

The graph is represented using a Python dictionary:

python
adj = { node: [list_of_neighbors] }

This structure enables:

  • O(1)O(1)O(1) access to a node’s neighbors

  • Efficient iteration during constraint checks

  • Compact memory usage compared to matrix representations

This format is used consistently across all algorithms to maintain uniformity.

Color Assignment Array

python
colors = [-1] * n

  • -1 indicates the vertex is uncolored

  • Once assigned, colors[v] = c stores the color index

  • This compact list representation simplifies color checking and merging results

Domain Dictionary for Forward Checking

python
domains = {i: set(range(k)) for i in range(n)}

Each vertex stores the set of colors that are currently legal given all prior assignments.
Forward Checking updates these sets dynamically during search.

Advantages:

  • Fast membership checking (color in domains[u])

  • Efficient pruning (removing a color is O(1)O(1)O(1))

  • Easy restoration by storing pruned values

Performance Counters

The solver records:

python
nodes_explored
backtracks
time_ms

  • nodes_explored: number of recursive calls

  • backtracks: number of failed branches

  • time_ms: total execution time in milliseconds

These metrics are required for Phase 2 experiments and comparative analysis (Section 6).

4.4.2 Variable Ordering: MRV Heuristic

A major optimization is the Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic. Instead of selecting vertices in a fixed order, the solver dynamically selects the vertex with the smallest remaining domain.

Implementation:

python
def select_mrv_node():
    uncolored = [v for v in range(n) if colors[v] == -1]
    return min(uncolored, key=lambda v: len(domains[v]))

Why MRV improves performance:

  • It selects the “hardest” vertex first

  • Forces conflicts earlier in the search

  • Reduces depth of the recursion tree

  • Decreases the number of backtracking steps

This matches classical CSP theory: fail early, prune large parts of the search space.

4.4.3 Constraint Propagation: Forward Checking

Forward Checking is applied immediately after assigning a color to a vertex. It removes the assigned color from all neighboring uncolored vertices’ domains.

Implementation summary:

python
removed = forward_check(node, color)
if removed is None:   # domain wiped out
    undo and continue

The FC routine:

  1. For each neighbor of node:

    • Remove the assigned color from its domain

  2. If any neighbor’s domain becomes empty, return failure

  3. Store all removed values so they can be restored when backtracking

Undoing FC:

python
undo_forward_check(removed)

FC benefits:

  • Detects infeasible partial colorings early

  • Prevents exploring entire subtrees that cannot lead to a solution

  • Complements MRV by tightening domains dynamically

4.4.4 Safety Check for Consistency

Before coloring a node with a particular color, the solver ensures no neighboring vertex already uses that color:

python
def is_safe(node, color):
    for neigh in adj[node]:
        if colors[neigh] == color:
            return False
    return True

This check prevents obvious conflicts and serves as an additional layer of constraint enforcement before FC.

4.4.5 Recursion Strategy

The solver follows a depth-first search:

  1. Check if all vertices are colored

  2. Select vertex using MRV

  3. Try each color in its domain

  4. Apply FC

  5. Recurse

  6. Undo assignments and domain reductions on failure

This mirrors classical CSP solvers, ensuring both completeness and optimality (the solver finds a valid coloring if one exists).

4.4.6 Time Measurement and Return Format

Execution time is measured using:

python
t0 = time.time()
...
t1 = time.time()

The solver returns results in a standardized dictionary:

python
{
    "coloring": {node: color} or None,
    "nodes_explored": nodes_explored,
    "backtracks": backtracks,
    "time_ms": (t1 - t0) * 1000
}

This standardized format allows:

  • Easy GUI integration

  • Automated graphing in experiments

  • Consistent comparison across algorithms

4.4.7 Practical Optimizations

OptimizationBenefit
MRVReduces branching factor and speeds up search
FCPrunes inconsistent assignments early
Domain cachingFast updates & reversals
Safe-check short-circuitPrevents unnecessary FC calls
Compact list-based coloringFast access and low overhead

Together, these optimizations elevate the algorithm from a naïve backtracking solution to an efficient exact solver suitable for the experimental comparison in Section 6.

import time

def solve_backtracking(adj, k, params=None):
    """
    Backtracking + MRV + Forward Checking for Graph Coloring.
    Returns:
      {
        "coloring": {node: color},
        "nodes_explored": int,
        "backtracks": int,
        "time_ms": float,
      }
    """

    n = len(adj)
    colors = [-1] * n  # -1 = uncolored

    # Domain for each node
    domains = {i: set(range(k)) for i in range(n)}

    nodes_explored = 0
    backtracks = 0

    def is_safe(node, color):
        """Check if node can take this color."""
        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == color:
                return False
        return True

    def select_mrv_node():
        """Choose uncolored node with minimum domain size."""
        uncolored = [i for i in range(n) if colors[i] == -1]
        if not uncolored:
            return None
        return min(uncolored, key=lambda x: len(domains[x]))

    def forward_check(node, color):
        """
        Forward checking: remove 'color' from neighbors' domains.
        Returns: removed_values for undo, OR None if failure.
        """
        removed = {}

        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == -1 and color in domains[neigh]:

                domains[neigh].remove(color)
                removed.setdefault(neigh, []).append(color)

                # Failure if domain becomes empty
                if len(domains[neigh]) == 0:
                    # must undo before returning None
                    for n2, vals in removed.items():
                        for v in vals:
                            domains[n2].add(v)
                    return None

        return removed

    def undo_forward_check(removed):
        """Undo domain pruning."""
        for node, vals in removed.items():
            for v in vals:
                domains[node].add(v)

    def backtrack():
        nonlocal nodes_explored, backtracks

        # STOP CONDITION
        if all(colors[i] != -1 for i in range(n)):
            return True

        nodes_explored += 1

        # Choose next node by MRV
        node = select_mrv_node()
        if node is None:
            return True

        # Try values from the domain
        for color in list(domains[node]):

            if is_safe(node, color):
                colors[node] = color

                removed = forward_check(node, color)

                if removed is not None:
                    if backtrack():
                        return True

                # Undo
                colors[node] = -1
                if removed is not None:
                    undo_forward_check(removed)

                backtracks += 1

        return False

    # Time measurement
    t0 = time.time()
    success = backtrack()
    t1 = time.time()

    result = {
        "coloring": None,
        "nodes_explored": nodes_explored,
        "backtracks": backtracks,
        "time_ms": (t1 - t0) * 1000,
    }

    if success:
        result["coloring"] = {i: colors[i] for i in range(n)}

    return result

python
import time


def solve_backtracking(adj, k, params=None):
    """
    Backtracking graph coloring with MRV + Forward Checking.

    :param adj: dict {node: [neighbors]}
    :param k:   maximum number of colors
    :param params: (unused for now, kept for consistency)
    :return: dict with keys:
             - "coloring": {node: color} or None if no solution
             - "nodes_explored": int
             - "backtracks": int
             - "time_ms": float (milliseconds)
    """

    n = len(adj)
    colors = [-1] * n  # -1 = uncolored

    # Domain for each node = all possible colors initially
    domains = {i: set(range(k)) for i in range(n)}

    nodes_explored = 0
    backtracks = 0

    def is_safe(node, color):
        """Check if we can assign this color to this node."""
        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == color:
                return False
        return True

    def select_mrv_node():
        """
        Select the uncolored node with the smallest domain size (MRV).
        """
        uncolored = [i for i in range(n) if colors[i] == -1]
        if not uncolored:
            return None

        # MRV = choose node with minimum domain size
        return min(uncolored, key=lambda node: len(domains[node]))

    def forward_check(node, color):
        """
        Apply forward checking after assigning a color.
        Remove `color` from domains of neighbors.
        If any neighbor domain becomes empty -> failure.
        Return: removed_values (to allow undo)
        """
        removed = {}

        for neigh in adj[node]:
            if colors[neigh] == -1 and color in domains[neigh]:
                domains[neigh].remove(color)
                removed.setdefault(neigh, []).append(color)

                # No available colors → fail early
                if len(domains[neigh]) == 0:
                    return None  # failure

        return removed  # success

    def undo_forward_check(removed):
        """Restore pruned domain values."""
        for node, vals in removed.items():
            for v in vals:
                domains[node].add(v)

    def backtrack():
        nonlocal nodes_explored, backtracks

        # Base case: all nodes colored
        if all(colors[i] != -1 for i in range(n)):
            return True

        nodes_explored += 1

        # Select variable using MRV
        node = select_mrv_node()
        if node is None:
            return True  # should not really happen if base case above holds

        # Try colors in the node domain
        for color in list(domains[node]):
            if is_safe(node, color):
                colors[node] = color

                # Forward checking
                removed = forward_check(node, color)

                if removed is not None:
                    if backtrack():
                        return True

                # Undo assignment
                colors[node] = -1

                # Undo domain pruning
                if removed is not None:
                    undo_forward_check(removed)

                backtracks += 1

        return False

    # Run
    t0 = time.time()
    success = backtrack()
    t1 = time.time()

    result = {
        "coloring": None,
        "nodes_explored": nodes_explored,
        "backtracks": backtracks,
        "time_ms": (t1 - t0) * 1000,
    }

    if success:
        result["coloring"] = {i: colors[i] for i in range(n)}

    return result
